passage:
After school, Vidya had spent a year "preparing" for an entrance exam. Mostly she slept late and scrolled her phone, and in the end she missed the exam date. Now every scholarship notice made her close the tab. "I don't deserve this. I wasted a whole year."
On the terrace one evening, her older cousin Rehana found her staring at a form. "What are you doing?"
"Nothing. I'm not applying. I threw my chance away."
"If your friend had done the same year, what would you tell her?"
Vidya was quiet for a long time. "That she was scared, and she did what she knew how to do then."
Rehana said nothing.
"I didn't know how to start," Vidya said slowly. The next morning she opened the form and read it to the end.

qa.q: What did Vidya miss after a year of preparing?
qa.a: Vidya missed the exam date.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling whenever a scholarship notice appeared?
qa.a: Vidya felt ashamed and undeserving, closing the tab and saying she had wasted a whole year.

qa.q: What turned things for Vidya on the terrace?
qa.a: Vidya imagined saying to a friend that she was scared and did what she knew how to do then. That let her see herself kindly and open the form.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen Vidya's silence after her question?
qa.a: Rehana likely saw that Vidya was thinking it through, so Rehana said nothing more and let her reach her own view.

grounding: A young adult who wasted a year punishes herself through lost opportunities, then sees the past self did the best it knew.

passage:
"You still haven't applied?" Nikita stirred her coffee. "The exchange closes Friday."
"I don't deserve it," Vishal said. "Not after what I did to Ananya."
"The library shouting?"
"That, and forgetting her birthday, and telling her she was boring. She cried. I was awful."
"That was unkind. Did you say sorry?"
"In March. She said thanks and that was it."
"So you've owned it. What would you say to a friend who did the same at twenty, stressed and not knowing better?"
Vishal thought. "That he'd do it differently now."
"Right. Now you can."
He was quiet, then pulled his laptop across the table. "Where's the link?"
"Bottom of the page."
"Thanks, Nikita." He started typing.

qa.q: When did Vishal apologise to Ananya?
qa.a: Vishal apologised in March.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he said he did not deserve the exchange?
qa.a: Vishal felt guilty and ashamed about how he treated Ananya, so much that he was ready to punish himself by skipping the exchange.

qa.q: What question did Nikita ask that helped Vishal move forward?
qa.a: Nikita asked what Vishal would say to a friend who did the same at twenty, stressed and not knowing better. Answering it let him see his past self more kindly.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Vishal's choice not to apply?
qa.a: Nikita seems to see it as extra punishment when Vishal has already apologised, and as something a person who has owned the harm no longer needs.

grounding: A young adult who hurt a partner keeps punishing himself through lost opportunities until seeing the past self did what it knew.

passage:
March: Akash sat in his room in Indore, surrounded by the engineering books he'd stopped opening a year ago. He'd spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon, then dropped out. Now he wouldn't apply anywhere. "Why should I get a second chance after wasting one?" he told his friend Tarun.
A week later: Tarun came over and asked, "What did you know then that you know now?" Akash was quiet a long time. "That I hated the course. That I didn't know how to say it." Tarun said, "So you were a nineteen-year-old doing the best you knew."
May: Akash filled in the form for a design diploma. His hands shook when he clicked submit. He still felt the old sting about that year, but he let himself apply anyway.

qa.q: How did Akash spend the year before he dropped out?
qa.a: He spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling in March when he refused to apply?
qa.a: He felt guilty and ashamed, believing he didn't deserve a second chance after wasting one.

qa.q: What small step helped Akash begin to forgive himself?
qa.a: Tarun's question about what he knew then, which helped Akash see his younger self as doing the best he knew rather than as someone to punish.

qa.q: How might Tarun have seen Akash's refusal to apply?
qa.a: Tarun probably saw it as punishment that kept Akash stuck, and cared enough to come over and gently question it.

grounding: Shows a young adult who punished himself for a wasted year learning that his past self did the best it knew, allowing him to move forward.

passage:
"Varun, I see you sitting with that rejection letter like it's a sentence from a judge," said Parul bua, settling on the sofa. "Let me tell you about me at twenty. I was with a boy in college and I was careless with him. I cancelled on him, I mocked his poems in front of friends. He ended it, and he was right to.
For two years after that I punished myself. I wouldn't let anyone close. I turned down the theatre group I loved because he'd been in it. I thought refusing good things was the least I deserved.
Then my Nani said something I've kept ever since: 'At twenty you did what you knew at twenty. Now you know more. Use it.' I wrote to him and apologised properly. Then I joined the theatre group. I was kinder in my next relationship because of him."

qa.q: What did Parul bua mock in front of friends?
qa.a: She mocked his poems in front of friends.

qa.q: What was Parul bua feeling during the two years after the breakup?
qa.a: She felt guilty and undeserving, refusing good things as a kind of punishment.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Parul bua move forward?
qa.a: Her Nani's words that at twenty she did what she knew at twenty; after that she apologised properly and joined the theatre group.

qa.q: How might the boy from college have felt on receiving her apology?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and respected, since she owned the hurt directly years later.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how she punished herself for hurting a partner until she saw her past self did what it knew and moved on.

passage: The audition hall had no power, the rain was hammering the tin roof, and the director was holding auditions by phone torch. Jahnavi stood outside the door, soaked, not going in. Two years ago, the night before the college play, she had panicked and walked out, leaving her team without a lead. She hadn't auditioned for anything since. "You don't get to be in plays after doing that," she told Avni, who had dragged her there. Avni pulled her under the awning. "What did you know then?" Jahnavi thought. "That I was scared. That I didn't know how to tell anyone." "So you were eighteen and panicking, and you did what you knew. You've already apologised to everyone." Jahnavi breathed. The rain didn't stop. She went in anyway, and did her monologue by torchlight.

qa.q: How was the director holding auditions?
qa.a: By phone torch, since the hall had no power.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling outside the audition door?
qa.a: She felt guilty and unworthy, believing that after walking out two years ago she didn't deserve to be in plays.

qa.q: How did Avni help Jahnavi move forward?
qa.a: Avni asked what Jahnavi knew then and reminded her she'd already apologised, helping her see her past self as scared, not bad.

qa.q: What would change if Jahnavi had kept punishing herself?
qa.a: She would keep losing chances she loves, like acting, without making anything better for her old team.

grounding: Shows a young adult who punished herself for a past failure learning that her younger self did what it knew, and moving forward.

passage: The scholarship form had sat on Nandini's desk in the Pune paying-guest room for eleven days. Maria picked it up. "Deadline's Friday. Why haven't you filled it?" "Because I wasted all of last year," Nandini said. "Skipped classes, slept till noon, failed two papers. People like me don't get to ask for things." Maria sat down on the bed. "You were nineteen and your dad had just moved away for work. What did you know then about handling that?" "Nothing," Nandini said slowly. "I didn't even know how to ask anyone for help." "So that girl did what she knew. You know more now." Nandini stared at the form for a long moment. Then she uncapped a pen and started on page one, hearing the old voice that said she hadn't earned it, and writing anyway.

qa.q: How long had the scholarship form sat on Nandini's desk?
qa.a: It had sat there for eleven days.

qa.q: Why hadn't Nandini filled in the form?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of wasting last year and believed she didn't deserve to ask for anything, so she kept punishing herself.

qa.q: Which question from Maria helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Nandini knew back then about handling it helped her see that her past self did what it could, so she could forgive it and act now.

qa.q: How might Maria see the old version of Nandini?
qa.a: Maria sees a nineteen-year-old struggling after a big change at home, not someone who should lose chances forever.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps punishing herself for a wasted year beginning to see that her past self did what it knew.
